payload.matrix_runs:
ONE run, degenerate by construction, recorded honestly. Datum: the strongest viable rival, which is today's shipped behaviour (merge everything, no tag, no branch commits) - not a hypothetical, since it is what the engine does right now. Candidate: 1a+2a+3a+4a+5a.

Run 1 against the datum: C1 nothing-lost - datum FAILS the veto (an empty branch closes as success, and nothing is ever committed to the branch), candidate PASSES (probed). C2 trunk-clean +1. C3 permanent name - datum FAILS the veto (no tag exists at all), candidate PASSES. C4 no-partial-state +1. C5 ordinary-mechanics 0, both use plain git. Net: two veto failures on the datum, +2 elsewhere, zero minuses.

No second run was performed, because a second run needs a surviving rival to become the new datum and there is none - the eleven alternatives were eliminated at M5 on stated failures. Recording one run and saying so is the honest form; iterating a matrix against itself would manufacture the appearance of convergence.

SENSITIVITY: the result is robust rather than weight-sensitive, and not because the weights are favourable - the datum fails two VETO criteria, so no reweighting of C2, C4 or C5 can flip it. The checkmark that would matter is not on a weight but on the veto itself: if the owner ever ruled that trunk-cleanliness outranks nothing-lost, the whole shape would change. That ruling is recorded the other way round in the goal system.
payload.winner:
Winner: the ruled design, implemented as 1a+2a+3a+4a+5a - merge --no-commit, drop the classified event paths from index and worktree, commit with both parents; classification by engine-held path rules; the milestone commit riding the existing bless window; the tag created before the merge; and closed iterations kept listable from the grant index.

WHY BEYOND THE ARITHMETIC. First, the arithmetic is not what decides it - the datum fails two veto criteria, which is a disqualification rather than a low score, and the qualitative reason is that today's behaviour can report success while doing nothing. Second, the choice is conservative where it matters: every mechanic is plain git, so the repository remains fully comprehensible to someone who has never heard of SE - which is the property that makes the record survive the tool. Third, the ordering inside the close was chosen for the failure case, not the success case: tag first, then merge, then filter, so that at every intermediate point the record is either fully in the tree or already named. Fourth, the tear between the per-bless lane and the once-only close means the expensive, safety-critical part can refuse without ever undoing work already committed. The honest weakness: with one candidate, this convergence proves the datum is unacceptable rather than proving this design is the best of several - and the design's own ruling, not this matrix, is what makes that acceptable.
